intro: Google Docs works well for medical writers on a Mac once you know the Mac keys. You work in a Chrome tab, and the shortcuts use ⌘ and ⌥ instead of Ctrl and Alt. This guide covers the keys, review tools, templates, size limits, offline use and review timelines, plus where Lazur helps.
tldr: Learn the Mac keys first. Google's shortcut page uses ⌘ and ⌥, and Tool finder opens with Option + /.
Run reviews in Suggesting mode with one owner for comments, so the change record stays clean.
Check the 1.02 million character limit and set up offline work in Chrome before a big review round.
Plan with AMWA's sample timelines, then add time for every extra reviewer.
Use Lazur for voice answers, drafts and dictation. It does not click buttons or edit files for you.

blocks.text: What medical writers use Google Docs for

Medical writers use Google Docs for shared drafts. The common jobs are clinical study reports, protocol amendments, investigator's brochures and review copies. If your company requires a controlled system for final files, use Docs for the messy middle, where several people comment on the same text.

AMWA, the American Medical Writers Association, lists Google Docs among the tools new writers should learn. Its career advice names Microsoft Word, Google Docs, PowerPoint, Excel and Adobe Acrobat as the tools of the profession. If you are new, get comfortable in Docs as well as Word.

Surveys give you a rough picture, not a verdict. The 2023 AMWA technology survey does not break out Google Docs or Word. So you cannot tell from it which tool wins in your team. What it does show is that most respondents already use technology in their work.
Google Docs shortcuts on a Mac

Google's shortcut page lists Windows and Mac keys side by side. On a Mac, Command (⌘) takes the place of Ctrl for most actions. Option (⌥) fills the role of Alt. Learn the short list below, then add more as you need them.

items: ⌘ + Shift + H opens Find and replace.
⌘ + Option + M inserts a comment.
⌘ + K inserts a link.
⌘ + Option + Shift + X switches the document to Suggesting.
⌘ + Down arrow moves you to the bottom of the document.
Option + / or Ctrl + Option + Z opens Tool finder.
Ctrl + Option + I opens the Insert menu.

blocks.text: Two things trip people up. First, menu access on a Mac uses Ctrl + Option, not Command. Second, some Mac shortcuts still use Ctrl, such as Ctrl + Shift + F to hide the menus. Read the key names before you press them.

Tool finder is the shortcut worth learning first. Google's page says it was formerly called 'Search the menus'. If a menu item has moved since you learned it, type the action into Tool finder instead of hunting through menus.
Shortcut lists on other sites disagree about Find and replace, so press ⌘ + Shift + H once in a scratch doc. Use Google's own page as your reference when the lists conflict.

blocks.title: Test in a scratch doc
blocks.text: Open a blank doc and press each shortcut once. If a key does nothing, search for the action in Tool finder. Finding the right key on a quiet afternoon beats finding it during a QC round.
Use Chrome for Docs when you can. Google's offline page names Chrome and Microsoft Edge only. If you plan to work offline on a Mac, Chrome is the safer default.
Suggesting mode and comments for review rounds

Suggesting mode is where review happens. Editing changes the text directly. Suggesting records each change as a proposal that the author can accept or reject. For a regulated document, that record matters, because you need to show who changed what.

Switch modes from the editing mode menu, or press ⌘ + Option + Shift + X. Ask reviewers to leave comments with ⌘ + Option + M. Put the mode rule in your kickoff note, so nobody edits clean text by accident.
A review round usually runs in four steps:

items: Make a copy of the draft and name it with the round number.
Set reviewers to Suggesting, so every change shows up as a proposal.
Reviewers add one issue per comment with ⌘ + Option + M.
The writer accepts or rejects each suggestion, then resolves the comment.

blocks.text: Example: a reviewer flags a dose unit in a table. They add a comment and suggest the corrected unit. The writer accepts the suggestion only after the source confirms it, then resolves the comment. The thread stays attached to the change.

Multiple reviewers slow the timeline. AMWA says more reviewers can add comments, slow the schedule and dilute responsibility. Name one person who makes the final call on each comment. Everyone else suggests and comments.

The clicks are on the how-to pages. Read [how to suggest edits in Google Docs](/how-to/suggest-edits-in-google-docs), then [how to accept or reject suggestions](/how-to/accept-or-reject-suggestions-in-google-docs). For comments, use [the comment guide](/how-to/add-a-comment-in-google-docs).
Templates for protocol amendments and clinical study reports

Templates save formatting time, but they need an owner. AMWA's working materials include company style guides, templates and previous document versions. Keep those in one shared Drive folder, so the next writer does not start from an old copy.

To open a template from inside a document, go to File > New > From a template. Pick one and click Insert. If the document already has content, the template opens in new tabs instead of replacing your text.

Example: you start a protocol amendment from last year's file. Open the new template in its own tab and paste the revised text there. The old version stays in the first tab for comparison, so nothing gets overwritten.

Some template features need a work or school account. Google's page says they are unavailable otherwise, and it links to sign-in. If your team uses personal accounts, ask your admin which template tools you can use.

Google's page does not cover custom templates or submitting them to an organization gallery. Check with your team before you build one. For the steps, use [the template guide](/how-to/create-a-template-in-google-docs).
File size, character limits and long documents

Google's Drive help page says a Google Doc can hold up to 1.02 million characters. A text document converted to Google Docs format can be up to 50 MB. Those are the two numbers to know before a big file moves in.

Check your own file against the character limit, not the page count. [See word count in Google Docs](/how-to/see-word-count-in-google-docs) for a live count. Then compare that count to 1.02 million characters.

Images are the open question. Google's page gives no image limit for Docs. Its only image cap covers Google Sites, at 15,000 images per site. So test a large, image-heavy file with your reviewers before the final round.

blocks.title: Keep raw data out
blocks.text: Docs is for text. Keep raw trial data in a locked system, and paste in only the summary tables you need. A shared doc full of raw data is harder to control.
Working offline on a Mac

Offline editing in Google Docs works in Chrome or Microsoft Edge. You need the Google Docs Offline Chrome extension, and private browsing blocks it. Google's offline page does not mention macOS or Safari. Do not assume a Safari setup will work on a plane.

Turn offline access on in Chrome while you still have a good connection. The steps are in [the offline mode guide](/how-to/turn-on-offline-mode-in-google-docs). Then test it once with the Wi-Fi off. You want to find problems at your desk, not on a train.
Expect to sync when you reconnect. Comments and suggestions from other people arrive after you are back online. Plan offline work as solo drafting, not live review.
Timelines for clinical and regulatory documents
Use AMWA's sample timelines to plan a review round. The numbers come from the sample AMWA used, so treat them as planning ranges for your team, not as a promise.

rows: Clinical study report with senior management review
blocks.caption: Sample timelines from the AMWA blog. Use them as planning ranges.

blocks.text: Here is a worked example. Say a protocol amendment starts with one draft and goes to three reviewers. AMWA's range for that document is 24 to 40 working days, so plan from the top of that range. Ask each reviewer for a date on day one, then compare those dates to the range.
AMWA also says compressed timelines leave less time for comments and fixes. Build the comment window into the plan from the start. Do not squeeze it in at the end.
Mistakes that slow down a review

items: Editing a live draft while reviewers still read an old copy. Make a copy, label it, and send only that.
Adding reviewers at the last minute. AMWA says more reviewers add comments and slow the timeline.
Pasting draft data into the shared file. AMWA says draft data can cause errors and version-control problems.
Mixing Editing and Suggesting. One silent edit to clean text breaks the review record.
Skipping a word count and a consistency pass before you send the file to QC.

blocks.text: Each of these costs days you do not get back. Fix the setup before the first comment lands, not after the third round of edits.
Consistency and QC checks in Google Docs
AMWA says a QC review generally covers 100% of the document. Its QC metrics include the number of QC findings, consistency errors and review rounds. You can track all three in a plain Google Doc.
Use Find and replace (⌘ + Shift + H) to hunt for every variant of a term. Search for 'mg/kg', then 'mg per kg', to catch mixed units. Repeat the search for drug names, arm labels and abbreviations.
Log the review rounds at the top of the file or in a small table. Write the round number, the date and the reviewer. It sounds dull. It saves you on the day QC asks what changed.

blocks.title: Dose checks stay manual
blocks.text: Lazur can read text out loud and help you draft. It does not check doses against your source data. Every number goes back to the source before the file leaves your desk.
Where Lazur fits in a Google Docs review

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Lazur sees your screen only while you hold the shortcut, so it can see the open doc.

It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for Google Docs or any other app. Use it beside the doc, not inside it. Think of it as a second reader who answers questions and points at things.

Use dictation for comment text. Hold fn and speak, and Lazur types clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Snippets and a personal dictionary help with words that autocorrect gets wrong, such as trade names and study codes.
Ask Lazur to draft a neutral reply to a reviewer. Lazur drafts and types the text. You read every word, change what needs changing, and send it yourself.
Research for background and public guidance

Research tasks run in Lazur's own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension. Lazur returns a summary and a report. Use it for public guidance and background reading, not for your own trial data.
Keep the source for every claim. Paste the URL into a comment on the sentence it supports. A reviewer can check it in seconds, and so can you next year.
Privacy and what leaves your Mac

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer your question. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.
Check your company policy before you use any AI tool on an unpublished draft. Many teams set their own rules about which tools can see trial documents. Ask your quality or privacy team first.

faq.question: Does Google Docs work on a Mac for medical writing?
faq.answer: Yes. Docs runs in a browser, and Google's help pages cover the Mac shortcuts with ⌘ and ⌥. Many medical writers use it for shared drafts and review rounds. Check your company's rules on where drafts can live before you start.

faq.question: Which Google Docs shortcut should a Mac user learn first?
faq.answer: Start with Tool finder, Option + / or Ctrl + Option + Z. It searches the menus for you, so you do not need every shortcut memorized. Then learn ⌘ + Option + M for comments and ⌘ + Option + Shift + X for Suggesting.

faq.question: Can I use Google Docs offline on a Mac?
faq.answer: Google's offline page lists Chrome and Microsoft Edge, with the Google Docs Offline Chrome extension. It does not mention macOS or Safari. Private browsing blocks offline access. Test it once with the Wi-Fi off before you travel.

faq.question: How large can a Google Doc be?
faq.answer: Google's Drive help page says up to 1.02 million characters. A text document converted to Google Docs format can be up to 50 MB. Google's page gives no image limit for Docs, so test image-heavy files early.

faq.question: Does Lazur edit my Google Doc for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps. It answers out loud, points at things, guides you one click at a time, and drafts or types text when you ask.

faq.question: Is Lazur a Google Docs add-on?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app. It answers out loud, points at things, and works beside the doc you have open.

faq.question: Does AMWA recommend Google Docs?
faq.answer: AMWA's career advice lists Google Docs with Microsoft Word, PowerPoint, Excel and Adobe Acrobat as tools new medical writers should learn. It does not rank them against each other.
